articles.title: I finally found a magnetic phone grip I never want to remove
articles.summary: The $50 OhSnap Snap Grip Stand is excellent and does what most magnet rings don’t — stand your phone vertically.
articles.body: I told myself I wouldn’t buy an OhSnap accessory for my phone. Every one I’d tested was nice, but felt overpriced and slightly flawed. After I weighed in on the $40 Snap Grip 5 last year, I wound up sticking with my $25 Syncwire instead. But OhSnap’s $50 Snap Grip Stand finally got me. To have a truly useful vertical stand and grip always attached to my phone, ready at a moment’s notice? Heck yes. [Media: I started testing the Snap Grip Stand months ago, and soon discovered that I never took it off. So I bought my own. It’s thin — 3.7mm, so it slips effortlessly into my pocket without making an extra indent in my pants. It’s got a double-sided magnetic ring, like the previous gen, so it not only sticks to your magnet ring phone, it can stick flat against a fridge or gym equipment or my garage cabinets. It even lets some wireless charging through. Like the previous gen, the magnets hold my phone tightly, and the grip part is one of the most versatile I’ve tried. The clever interlocking joints can fit between two of your fingers loosely like a PopSocket, or you can put a finger through the joints for a very secure grip. The whole disc spins freely (though still with a bit of scraping noise) to rotate to any angle you like. But unlike the previous gen, the Stand has a stand unlike most other magnet grips on the market. The entire magnet ring is now encircled by a thinner fold-out ring on a hinged arm. Pull it down, and it effortlessly props up my phone in its normal vertical orientation. Most rival stands barely prop a phone, and even then they don’t deploy as fast. Here, there’s no need to take off the stand, or rotate it and lock a tab in place like OhSnap’s previous grips — pull out, plop phone on surface, done. [Image: OhSnap advertises that it’s “thinner than your camera bumps,” but that depends on whether you’re using a case. It’s thin enough. It’s not the only stand with such a design. The $17 Gornergrat Grat 5 has a similar stand and costs far less. But I tried one and found I don’t like its elastic strap, which feels loose and thus less secure around my fingers. OhSnap makes use of the extra vertical arm space to keep the stand from rotating when you don’t want it to: It’s got a extra vertical magnet in there to match Apple’s MagSafe pattern, as well as some grippy clear plastic material to provide friction. And I’m happy to say the aluminum gadget doesn’t seem to have any other unwanted coatings: I wasn’t a fan of the adhesive on the Snap Grip 4, or the soft-touch coating that started to peel when I tested the Snap Grip 5. Here, it appears to be bare anodized metal that looks and feels great. [Image: Neither of these phones (Pixel 9, Galaxy S25) has built-in magnets, but I bought magnet cases for each. Phone grips like this also come with adhesive magnet rings. Right now, I can only think of three things that’d make it better: a lower price, magnets in the stand’s ring (rather than the main ring) so I can use the magnets and the stand at the same time, and maybe a better way to open the grip one-handed. I do like how Tango’s spring-loaded grip can pop open when you press it. But I tried a Tango too, and I don’t like the way that spring feels between my fingers, pushing them apart too much. As for the lower price, at least OhSnap’s products are regularly on sale. I bought mine at Best Buy for $40 after tax.

articles.title: Don’t overlook Elektron’s budget electronic music instruments
articles.summary: Elektron’s Model:Samples and Model:Cycles are criminally slept-on electronic music instruments that are more powerful and fun than their bargain price suggests.
articles.body:
When I’m asked what to buy if you want to get into making electronic music, I often recommend Elektron’s budget-minded Model:Samples and Model:Cycles grooveboxes. They don’t grab headlines the way Teenage Engineering’s gear or the Telepathic Instruments Orchid do, and even compared to the company’s higher-end and more niche musical offerings like the Digitakt, Octatrack, or Tonverk, they’re often overlooked. But as my collection has grown to include fancier and far more expensive instruments, I still find myself coming back to the Model series. Those looking to get their first groovebox are often drawn to more familiar brand names like Korg or Roland. And lots of people on Reddit will be quick to recommend the Novation Circuit Tracks (which I personally find confusing and mediocre-sounding). This is probably also partially due to the reputation Elektron gear has for being obtuse. If you’re an established music maker and aren’t deterred by a complicated workflow, you’re probably going to pick up a more powerful Elektron box, like the Digitone or Syntakt. That leaves the Models lineup in a weird no man’s land, and that’s a shame. The primary difference between the two Models instruments is that the Model:Cycles uses FM synthesis and the Model:Samples, appropriately enough, plays samples. (It is not technically a sampler, however, since it can’t record samples, and instead they have to be loaded over USB.)  [Image: Connectivity isn’t the Model:Cycles’ strong suit. The Model:Cycles is built around a streamlined version of the engine found in the Digitone, one of my favorite-sounding synths of all time. This is a modern take on FM that can do the cold bells and icy pads you associate with iconic instruments like the DX7 (the iconic sound of the ’80s). But it also does modern glassy keys and aggressive turn-of-the-millennium EDM bass. The two are more alike than not, though. They’re both six-track grooveboxes with six velocity-sensitive pads and plenty of knobs for hands-on controls, and they look almost identical. But most importantly, they feature Elektron’s legendary step sequencer without being nearly as intimidating as the company’s more expensive and notoriously complicated offerings. The sequencer is built around what the company calls “trigs” and “locks.” Trigs are basically just events, typically triggering a note, and locks are just step-specific settings. It seems like a simple enough concept, but it makes these instruments far more capable than they might seem at first blush.

Six tracks isn’t a lot to work with. Once you’ve loaded up a kick, snare, and hi-hat, then you’ve only got three more tracks for bass, any melodic elements, and additional percussion. But sound locks allow you to change samples or presets on a per-step basis. That means, so long as they never play simultaneously, you can have your kick and snare share the same track, then you can put your hi-hats and other percussion on a second track, and leave the four other tracks for everything else. This is just the most obvious example of how locks expand the possibilities of what might seem rather limited on paper. The sequencer can be treated like a simple step sequencer where you drop a four-on-the-floor kick and a snare on the backbeat. But it also grows with you as your skills improve, and you want to create more complex tracks. Trig conditions, for example, allow you to set rules that govern when certain steps are triggered, like only every third time through the loop, only when you press the fill button, or only if a previous trig condition is met. This means that you can create a huge amount of variety in a single 64-step pattern. And then you can chain several of those patterns together to create complex and evolving arrangements that just aren’t possible on most gear in this price range. [Image: There’s plenty of hands-on controls for jamming. The Models boxes are also just incredibly fun. Where Elektron’s other gear demands a lot of menu diving, the Model:Samples and Model:Cycles are immediately approachable and built for live performance. It’s easy to trigger a drum fill with the push of a button, tweak a knob to open the filter on a bass, or briefly bathe a lead melody in delay.  Control-all might be the most fun feature, which, as you might have guessed, allows you to control all the tracks simultaneously. Bury your entire track in reverb as you start cranking up the distortion and lowering the pitch of all your samples to create a mangled, chaotic breakdown. And then immediately undo it all and drop the beat again by pressing the function and pattern buttons. The Model:Samples and Model:Cycles encourage jamming in a way that frankly a lot of electronic music gear just doesn’t, and it’s an absolute blast. Now, they’re not without their flaws. The pads are pretty mediocre. Having to load samples via USB rather than recording them directly kinda sucks. And the lack of polyphony (each sequencer track can only play one note at a time) is a bit of a bummer. But at $349, it’s hard to complain. Plus they can be snagged used for as little as $200 on Reverb or Craigslist. Frankly, they’re some of the best bargains in music hardware and a great place to start your journey into producing electronic music.

articles.title: 7 desk gadgets that can make your workday better
articles.summary: The right desk gadgets can help you reduce clutter, stay focused, and add a little extra convenience to your day.
articles.body:
We spend dozens of hours at our desks each week (if not more), so it’s worth creating a workspace that’s productive and enjoyable. The right desk gadgets can help you reduce clutter, stay focused, and add a little extra convenience to your day.

From ambient lighting to smart mugs, there are a lot of products designed to make the time you spend at your desk better, so we’ve combined a list of some options. Whether you’re working from home or in an office, these gadgets can help transform your workspace.

The Anker Nano Charging Station combines plugs, USB-C, and USB-A ports with retractable charging cables into a single compact charger. The station has a 1.3-inch LCD screen that displays real-time power output and temperature.

You can charge a laptop, phone, tablet, earbuds, and other devices on the same station, getting off the need for multiple chargers around your workspace. The retractable cables make it easy to plug in a device when needed without cluttering up your desk with extra wires.

The white model is available with $10 off for Prime Members at Amazon .

Logitech Lift Vertical Ergonomic Wireless Mouse — $80

If you’re working at your desk all day, a standard mouse can be hard on your wrist. The Logitech Lift Vertical Mouse is designed to promote a more natural posture in the forearm. It’s a good fit for small to medium hands, and there’s also a left-handed option available.

The vertical mouse has six customizable buttons that offer quick access to shortcuts, and connects wirelessly via Bluetooth or with the included USB receiver.

The Odistar desktop vacuum is an affordable option for keeping your desk clean and crumb-free, especially if you often eat meals at your desk. You can also use it to clean your keyboard and remove dust and debris between keys.

It’s quiet and simple to use, and because it’s so compact, you can keep it on your desk or tuck it away in a drawer until you need it. It’s cordless and uses two AA batteries. At just $13 , the desktop vacuum is a great way to keep your desk clean as you work.

If you’re someone who enjoys hot coffee but often finds yourself drinking it cold after getting sidetracked while working, the Ember Mug 2 can help keep your drinks at the perfect temperature.

You can set an exact temperature using your phone and the smart mug maintains it for up to one and a half hours with the 10-ounce version and up to 80 minutes with the 12-ounce version. The mug allows for a more consistent coffee experience, making your workday more enjoyable.

The Amazon Echo Dot can be a great addition to your work desk as you can use voice commands to set reminders, create to-do lists, check your calendar, play music, adjust smart lights, or get quick answers to questions without having to reach for your phone.

Because it’s small, you can easily place it anywhere on your desk where it can act as a hands-free assistant that helps keep you organized and focused throughout your workday.

The Govee Glide Hexa Light Panels are a simple and fun way to add some personality to your work desk setup without taking up any actual desk space. The hexagon-shaped panels mount on the wall behind your monitor and can display different colors and customizable lighting effects through the Govee app .

They can be used to create a focused atmosphere during work hours and can be switched to more dynamic effects when gaming or taking a break. The panels can be arranged in different patterns to match your style.

If you’re someone who hasn’t yet delved into the world of fidget toys but often finds yourself playing with random objects or even wrappers during calls or meetings, Speks might be for you. They’re tiny magnets that you can fidget or build with to keep your brain focused and your hands busy.

Instead of fidgeting with whatever happens to be within reach, you can have something that is actually made for the job and is more satisfying to have in your hands. They can help you stay focused and relieve stress throughout your workday.

This post originally published July 5 and has been updated with additional products.

articles.title: 8 things we learned from Google's Pixel 11 event
articles.summary: Google's Pixel 11 lineup introduces Magic Capture, HiLight notifications and proactive Gemini features designed to reduce screen time demands.
articles.body: Google packed a lot into its annual Made by Google event Aug. 12.  We got four Pixel 11 phones, a new Pixel Watch, Google's first finder tag and fresh Pixel Buds features. Yet one theme kept coming through. Google wants its devices to anticipate what you need before you have to ask. I was especially interested in what these upgrades could change in everyday use. A faster processor sounds nice. A phone that surfaces your flight information when someone texts you about a trip feels much more personal. FBI HELPS TAKE DOWN AI PHISHING RING If you want to see how much has changed in one generation, take a look back at our coverage of the Pixel 10 event and Google's previous phones, smartwatch and earbuds.  Here are the eight things that stood out to me. New! Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers.  No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward. Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com. 1) Google's Pixel 11 lineup gets meaningful upgrades The phone lineup includes the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL and Pixel 11 Pro Fold. All four use Google's new Tensor G6 processor and are designed around its latest Gemini Intelligence features. The standard Pixel 11 gets a camera bar that is 40% thinner than earlier base-model Pixels. It also has a larger 48-megapixel main camera with 56% more light sensitivity than the Pixel 10. Its 5x telephoto camera now supports up to 30x Super Zoom.  The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL have Google's brightest Pixel displays yet, reaching up to 3,600 nits. Google also says a new display coating provides more than twice the scratch resistance of the previous Pro generation. Its upgraded telephoto camera can reach up to 120 times Pro Zoom.  All three traditional Pixel 11 models now start with 256 GB of storage. Google also carries Pixelsnap magnetic wireless charging into the Pixel 11 lineup, with Qi2 support and faster wireless charging that can reach up to 25W on compatible models. Pixelsnap lets you snap on compatible chargers, stands, grips and other magnetic accessories. Then there is the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Google made it almost 10% lighter and about 1 millimeter thinner than the Pixel 10 Pro Fold. A redesigned hinge, new back material and stronger outer display also make it three times more durable than last year's Fold, according to Google's testing. That gives the Pixel 11 family a clearer reason to upgrade beyond AI alone. Google has changed the cameras, durability and charging experience while refining the physical design. Google is also trying to make switching from an iPhone less painful. Quick Share on Pixel can now send and receive photos and videos with iPhones and MacBooks, while Google says your photos and group chats can move over when you switch. All four Pixel 11 phones are available for preorder now, including the Google Pixel 11, Google Pixel 11 Pro, Google Pixel 11 Pro XL and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold. They officially go on sale Aug. 20. 2) Gemini gets much more proactive on Pixel 11 Google is taking another step toward making Gemini feel less like an app you open and more like something that can help across your phone. Gemini can now handle multistep tasks across more than 40 apps. Pixel 11 can also surface information based on what you are doing.  For example, if a friend messages you about an upcoming trip, a card can appear with your booking information and flight status. Pixel can also suggest actions based on your conversation. If you are discussing dinner plans, for example, it may offer a prompt to make a reservation. It can suggest adding an event to Calendar or saving a location to Maps. Google also introduced Rambler, a Gemini-powered voice input feature. It cleans up natural speech as it transcribes you. That means filler words such as "um" and "ah" do not have to end up in your finished message. That could be one of those small features you quickly start using every day. Much of this is powered by Google's new Tensor G6 processor. Google says Tensor G6 can process on-device AI tasks up to 3.5 times faster while using up to 3.5 times less energy than the previous generation under its testing. Google also introduced Sign To Text, which lets Pixel understand American Sign Language through the camera. Users can sign to write, chat or prompt Gemini from the keyboard. Google says the feature can recognize one-handed and two-handed signing along with facial expressions for grammar and tone. It is available for ASL now, with more sign languages planned. 3) Pixel 11 cameras want you to stop staring at the screen One of my favorite ideas from the event is Magic Capture. Instead of making you concentrate on hitting the shutter at exactly the right second, Magic Capture can analyze around 400 frames during a typical session. It then delivers carefully timed 12-megapixel photos. The feature can also automatically crop or unblur an image. At the same time, it saves video without making you switch camera modes. That could come in handy with kids, pets or anything else that refuses to pose for you. The hardware gets an upgrade too. Pixel 11 has a new 48-megapixel main sensor that Google says delivers 56% more light sensitivity than Pixel 10. Its 5x telephoto camera can reach 30x Super Zoom. Meanwhile, Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL get an upgraded 48-megapixel telephoto camera. Google says its larger sensor provides 30% more light sensitivity. The Pro phones can reach up to 120x Pro Zoom. Google says the new Instant Night Sight is four times faster, helping Pixel capture low-light photos without requiring you to hold the phone still as long.  There is also a new Camera Looks feature. It lets you choose a visual style before taking the photo. You can select a default look or customize additional styles to suit the shot. If the camera is your biggest reason for upgrading a phone, you may also want to compare the new Pixels with our current top Android phones of 2026 at cyberguy.com. 4) HiLight brings back the notification light with a twist Remember when phones had little notification lights? Google is bringing that idea back in a much more noticeable way. Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL introduce HiLight. Colored LED lights around the camera flash can glow while the phone is face down. For example, HiLight uses different patterns to show when Gemini is listening, thinking or responding. You can also assign colors to important contacts so an incoming call gives you a visual clue about who is calling. Google says message notifications from favorite contacts are among the capabilities planned for HiLight later. I like the thinking here. Phones are very good at pulling us back onto the screen. A quick visual signal could give you useful information without demanding your full attention. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold gets HiLight as well. 5) Pixel 11 puts more control around AI and security With Gemini getting access to more context on your phone, privacy was an obvious question at the event. Google says Pixel gives users visibility into what AI is doing and controls over how their data is used. You can also turn AI features on or off. Google highlighted several security protections built into Pixel 11. The phone can automatically block many spam calls and texts while warning you about messages or calls that may be scams. Google is also promising seven years of automatic security updates. An upgraded security chip is designed to help protect personal information stored on the phone. 6) Pixel Watch 5 moves deeper into health monitoring Pixel Watch 5 may be the device I would watch most closely after launch. Google upgraded its GPS and says route tracking can be twice as accurate as previous Pixel Watch generations in difficult environments. The watch also gets 50% more RAM and a faster processor compared with Pixel Watch 4.  Then there is Google Health. Pixel Watch 5 introduces Health Guardian features that look for longer-term changes in your wellness. These include monthly summaries involving blood pressure trends, sleep breathing quality and insulin resistance trends. Google says these features are designed for general wellness and are not intended to diagnose or treat medical conditions. The headline safety feature is Breathing Emergency Detection. It uses the watch's sensors and on-device AI to look for a severe, persistent drop in oxygen saturation. If the wearer becomes unresponsive, the watch can automatically call emergency services and transmit the person's location.  There is an important catch for U.S. buyers. Breathing Emergency Detection is available on Pixel Watch 4 and Pixel Watch 5 in select European countries. It is not available in the United States. Google says it plans to expand the feature to more countries. Pixel Watch 5 is available for preorder now and starts at $399 for the 41 mm model and $429 for the 45 mm version. The watches go on sale Aug. 20. 7) Pixel Tag finally gives Google its own item tracker Google is officially entering the finder-tag business. Pixel Tag is a small tracker for things such as keys, wallets or luggage. It connects to Google's Find Hub network, which includes more than 1 billion Android devices. That network can help locate an item when your own phone is no longer nearby.  When you are close to the tag, Ultra-Wideband with Bluetooth Channel Sounding can provide distance and directional guidance on compatible devices. You can also make the Pixel Tag play a sound. Interestingly, the button on the tag works in reverse too. Press it and you can ring your phone. Google says the replaceable battery lasts more than one year. The tag carries an IP67 water and dust resistance rating. You can also share a Pixel Tag with up to 10 people. Security matters with any location tracker. Google says Android phones automatically warn you if an unknown tag appears to be traveling with you. We have covered Google's expanding location tools before. You can read more about Find Hub and Google's Android security protections. Pixel Tag costs $29 for one or $99 for a four-pack. It is not available for preorder yet. Google says it goes on sale Nov. 11. WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME 8) Pixel Buds Pro 2 get smarter without buying new earbuds Google did not replace the Pixel Buds Pro 2. Instead, it announced new software features and a new Olive finish. Google says an upgraded Active Noise Cancellation feature can compensate when the fit or seal changes, helping maintain noise cancellation while you are moving. Another clever feature connects the Buds with Pixel Watch. Later this year, your Buds will automatically pause audio if your Pixel Watch senses that you have fallen asleep. Google also says Live Translate improvements are coming to Pixel Buds Pro 2 and Pixel Buds 2a later this fall. Pixel Buds Pro 2 are also getting the new Olive color to complement this year's Pixel devices. The Pixel Buds Pro 2 are available now, with the new Olive color joining the lineup. Kurt's key takeaways Google could have spent its Pixel 11 launch talking mainly about faster processors and brighter displays. Instead, some of the most interesting changes focus on reducing how much attention your devices demand. Magic Capture could make it easier to get the photo without experiencing the entire moment through your screen. HiLight could tell you whether a call matters before you pick up your phone. I am also watching the Pixel Watch 5 closely. A watch that can automatically call for help during certain breathing emergencies could become an important safety tool. However, U.S. buyers need to know that feature is not available here yet. Pixel Tag feels overdue, especially given the size of Google's Find Hub network. Still, proactive Gemini may be the biggest shift. Your phone can increasingly use context from your apps and conversations to decide what information might help you next. That could save time, but it also makes understanding your privacy settings more important. How much should your phone know about what you are doing in order to predict what you need next? Would you welcome that kind of help or rather have Gemini wait until you ask? articles.title: Sonos finally added Live Activities controls for your iPhone lockscreen
articles.summary: The latest update to the Sonos app adds support for iOS Live Activities, putting basic controls and info on your lockscreen.
articles.body: Sonos released an update to its mobile app that finally introduces support for iOS’ Live Activities, giving iPhone users quick access to playback controls on their lockscreen. The added functionality is a “much requested, anticipated, and needed feature,” according to a post Sonos shared to Reddit today that was spotted by 9to5Mac. While some features like displaying album art are not available, the Sonos Live Activity provides basic details and controls when listening to music or podcasts through a Sonos system without having to fully unlock your iPhone and open the app.  Support for Live Activities and lockscreen controls similar to what’s already available in the Android version of the Sonos app was teased by the company’s CEO Tom Conrad during an interview with Bloomberg last February. And following backlash to a major Sonos app update in 2024, support for Live Activities is off by default but can be enabled by navigating to both the Sonos app’s preferences as well as the Sonos app section of iOS’ settings. Once it’s turned on, the Live Activity will appear “after you initiate playback and then close the app” and displays the name of the group or room where audio was last playing from and the title of what you’re listening to. After playback stops, the Live Activity will automatically disappear from your lockscreen after 15 minutes. Support for the Apple Watch and CarPlay is included, but while the Live Activity will be displayed on your wrist or in your car, the controls aren’t supported there. It’s not known if or when those controls will ever work, but Sonos says its team is still working to improve the new feature, and when it comes to album art, the company is exploring “alternative ways to enhance the lock screen experience.”

articles.summary: We may have our first glimpse of Apple’s rumored camera-equipped AirPods, thanks to a demo video pulled from the macOS Tahoe 26.7 Release Candidate.
articles.body: We may have our first glimpse of Apple’s rumored camera-equipped AirPods, thanks to a video that MacRumors found in the macOS Tahoe 26.7 Release Candidate. The short video clip features a man — who is wearing the new AirPods — holding up a book with the cover displayed, so that Visual Intelligence can see the book title.  A Siri voice-over plays over the clip, saying “with Visual Intelligence, your world becomes savable. See something you like? Just ask me to save it for later.” Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman has previously reported that the rumored AirPods with cameras are designed to take in “visual information in low resolution” and act as eyes for Apple’s AI features, potentially allowing Siri to give turn-by-turn directions or answer questions about the wearer’s surroundings. The AirPods shown in the new demo clip look like a slightly thicker version of the AirPods Pro 3. That’s what Gurman had predicted, along with longer stems to accommodate the cameras, and LED lights that indicate when data is being uploaded to the cloud. We only get a look at the AirPods from the back in the video, but no lights can be seen on them from that angle. [Media: Given those Visual Intelligence features, the AirPods are poised to compete with other camera-equipped AI gadgets like Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, though Apple is also reportedly working on its own smart glasses too. While the AirPods’ cameras “aren’t designed” to snap photos or videos, the stealthy form factor may exacerbate the existing privacy concerns surrounding camera-equipped AI products, following Meta’s “pervert glasses” backlash. For now, details about Apple’s AirPods with cameras are still slim. If demo videos are already making their way into Apple’s OS betas, the new AirPods may launch alongside the improved version of Siri, which is expected to arrive in September together with the next generation of iPhones.

articles.title: Fairphone is launching its latest repairable phone in the US too | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The Fairphone 6+ is a midrange Android offering, but given the increasing prices of consumer gadgets amid the ongoing component shortages, a repairable device that can be made to last for years may prove a good proposition.
articles.body:
Fairphone, the Dutch company known for its sustainable and repair-friendly phones, on Tuesday said its latest smartphone, Fairphone (Gen 6+), is now available in the U.S., starting at $649.

The company previously had a partnership with French open source operating system maker e/OS to sell a “de-Googled” version of its previous smartphones in the States, but this is the first time people in the U.S. can buy the company’s phones directly without any modifications. The company said the Fairphone 6+ will support T-Mobile and AT&T at launch.

The Fairphone 6+ is strictly a midrange Android offering, but given the increasing prices of consumer gadgets amid the ongoing component shortages, a repairable device that can be made to last for years may prove a good proposition.

“We’re delivering a device built from the ground up to be opened, repaired, and kept alive for many years,” Fairphone CEO Raymond van Eck said.

The Fairphone 6+ runs on Qualcomm’s midrange Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 processor and has 12GB of RAM. The phone has a 4,415 maAh battery with support for 30 W fast-charging. It features a 6.31 LTPO OLED display with an adaptive refresh rate of up to 120 Hz.

As for photography, the phone’s main camera has a 50-megapixel Sony sensor with an f/1.88 aperture, and the secondary camera has a 13-megapixel ultrawide sensor with an f/2.2 aperture. The selfie camera on the front is a 32-megapixel sensor with an f/2.0 aperture.

Personally, I would have preferred a telephoto camera instead of an ultrawide for a two-camera setup. On paper, these cameras look like they would be good enough to take photos in the daylight, but in low light, expect the performance to dwindle.

The Fairphone’s 12 replaceable parts are the main selling points, however. These include important components like the battery, cameras, USB-C port, and the display, which can be swapped out using a single screwdriver. The company offers five years of warranty and software support until 2033.

Fairphone claims it also focuses on keeping its manufacturing process sustainable. The company said it was able to reduce the carbon footprint to 30 kg of CO2e for each Fairphone 6+ it manufactured.

The Fairphone 6+ is available in Forest Green, Horizon Black, and Cobalt Blue. The company is also selling accessories like a finger loop, lanyard, and card holder, which users can install by removing the back cover.

articles.title: Apple's new macOS update reportedly contains a video of AirPods with a camera | TechCrunch

Apple seems to be preparing launch materials for its upcoming AirPods with a camera, a leaked video in the latest macOS update spotted by MacRumors suggests.

The video, found in macOS 26.7 RC, shows a man holding up a book and talking with Siri about it using visual information.

“With Visual Intelligence, your world becomes savable. See something you like? Just ask me to save it for later,” the voiceover in the video says.

MacRumors reports that these new AirPods have a camera that can be used to examine objects in front of the user and answer questions about it. The publication apparently found a line in the software code that suggests the AirPods will notify you if your hair or something else is covering the camera.

In May, Bloomberg reported that Apple was in the late stages of testing such a device. The report said the camera-equipped AirPods would look like the AirPods Pro 3, but will have a longer stem and an LED light to indicate that data is being sent to the cloud.

Other devices, like the Ray-Ban Meta Glasses, Looki pendant, and smart glasses from Rokid , already do something similar. This might be Apple’s move to embed real-world intelligence into devices before it launches smart glasses of its own.

Bloomberg noted that Apple wanted to release the new AirPods in the first half of 2026, but now that it will ship the new Siri in September, it will look to launch them along with the operating system updates.

articles.title: Why Apple's camera-equipped AirPods may not be the 'pervert pods' consumers fear | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Apple’s leaked camera-equipped AirPods might avoid the privacy pitfalls of other AI wearables by preventing users from recording photos and videos.
articles.body:
Camera-equipped AI wearables today have developed a bit of a reputation problem. Devices like Meta’s Ray-Bans raise concerns about people being recorded without their consent. So the idea that Apple is reportedly preparing to release AirPods with cameras in them seems to conflict with the iPhone maker’s desire to position itself as a privacy-focused tech company.

But Apple’s now-leaked camera-equipped AirPods may not be as creepy as they first sound.

The rumored cameras were reportedly confirmed via video footage found in Apple’s macOS 26.7 RC (short for “release candidate,” or the final test version of the software before it ships publicly). The footage, found by researcher Aaron Perris , shows a man holding up a book while wearing AirPods and apparently having a conversation with Siri about it.

The audio track accompanying the video says: “With Visual Intelligence, your world becomes savable. See something you like? Just ask me to save it for later.”

The addition of cameras to the popular wireless earbuds is further confirmed through code that references a “Hair Detected” error, which would warn users when their hair is covering the AirPods’ camera. The launch of such a device could very easily backfire on Apple if not done right.

For a company whose brand is built on trust, this is a bigger gamble for Apple than one of its typical hardware refreshes. AirPods currently blend as a simple iPhone accessory that people wear all day without a second thought. A change like this could instead push them to the front of people’s minds, making them wonder whether the person opposite them is secretly recording.

Apple appears to have thought this through, based on prior reporting. According to an earlier report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman , the AirPods with cameras won’t be able to record media. As Gurman put it:

The cameras essentially act as eyes for the Siri digital assistant and aren’t designed to take photos or video. These components — located in both the right and left earbuds — allow the device to capture visual information in low resolution.

In other words, the goal isn’t to turn one of Apple’s best-selling accessories into a surveillance device (lest they become “pervert pods”). It’s to provide a way for AirPods owners to engage with the newly upgraded Siri AI, which is set to ship in September with Apple’s iOS 27 and other software updates.

That means an AirPods wearer could look at something — like a book, as shown in the leaked video, or perhaps some ingredients they’re preparing to cook, per Gurman’s earlier reporting — and simply ask Siri for help. The feature could also be useful for turn-by-turn walking directions when navigating an unfamiliar city.

For Apple, the bigger strategic bet is that this feature could also push consumers toward, if not a screen-free future entirely, then at least one where there’s less need to pull out an iPhone throughout the day. By baking AI access into a commonly worn and already socially acceptable wearable, Apple’s customers could interact with the world around them in a more natural way than staring down at a glowing screen.

There is one wrinkle, though. Gurman also reported that the new AirPods would include an LED indicator that lights up whenever the device is sharing visual data to the cloud. He questioned the light’s visibility, given the AirPods’ small size, but either way, its inclusion could work against Apple. Though it’s the right thing to do from a transparency and privacy perspective, that LED risks visually lumping AirPods in with other AI wearables already facing public skepticism, like the Meta Ray-Bans , Snap’s Specs , or Google’s new AI glasses . Apple can control what the cameras do, but it’ll have far less control over what people assume they do.

articles.title: Tesla is finally launching the Cybercab — let’s hope it’s ready
articles.summary: Tesla is getting ready to launch its Cybercabs as part of its Robotaxi service. But the driverless vehicle’s software raises a lot of safety questions.
articles.body: The Tesla Cybercab, that golden two-seater central to Elon Musk’s robo-supremacist ambitions, is finally nearing its public launch. Whether or not the no-steering wheel and no-pedal vehicle is actually ready for public roads, let alone customers, remains very much in doubt. According to The Information, Tesla is planning a public launch of the Cybercab in Austin, Texas, as soon as this month. The driverless vehicle has been popping up around the country, although often with a steering wheel and pedals, as employees are continuing to gather data. Tesla employees have been testing the fully driverless version on private roads around the company’s campus since July. And it recently completed a training with first responders in Austin, teaching them how to move the vehicles in the event of an emergency, Brad Cesak, a spokesperson for the city of Austin, confirmed. Tesla’s Robotaxi account on X recently confirmed that a “Cybercab launch event” was imminent, inviting followers to take a ride in the company’s Model Y robotaxis in order to win a ticket. [Media: But given what we know about Tesla’s autonomous driving project so far, the Cybercab could be heading for trouble. The Cybercab operates using Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) software, which the company claims is significantly safer than human driving. However, independent safety experts and federal regulators have called into question this claim, noting that FSD requires constant driver oversight and remains under active investigation by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration for traffic compliance failures. Over a year after its launch, Tesla’s Robotaxi service still uses human safety monitors in some markets. But the Cybercab is designed to operate without any human intervention, which removes one layer of safety on which Tesla can fall back. The company says it employs remote operators who can take control in case of an emergency, but experts question whether signal strength and latency could hamper reactions, especially during incidents in which every second counts. Tesla recently started adding Starlink to its Cybercabs to address this question of connectivity. There’s also the question of data, and whether Tesla has enough of the right kind. For years, Tesla was assumed to have an advantage in the race to put driverless cars on the road, thanks to the millions of vehicles on the road, passively gathering data to help train its autonomous driving models. But the Cybercab is a different type of vehicle with a unique platform that requires its own specialized data, Musk said during an earnings call in July. “We need to accumulate driving data that is specific to the Cybercab before we can put a lot of them on the road,” he said. Once considered to be a leader in data collection, Tesla may actually be a laggard. During that same earnings call, Ashok Elluswamy, the company’s head of AI, said that Tesla’s unsupervised robotaxis have driven 380,000 miles across six cities in two different states. Waymo, which has operated a commercial robotaxi service since 2020, has driven over 220 million fully driverless miles on public roads — or about 579 times more miles than Tesla. Tesla uses a mix of unsupervised and supervised vehicles as part of its current Robotaxi fleet, but that ratio appears to be in a constant state of flux. According to the crowdsourced Robotaxi Tracker, the company was operating 16 unsupervised vehicles in Austin, four in Dallas, and one in Houston. Tesla also hasn’t submitted its safety claims for independent analysis, instead relying on self-published statistics while actively working to block public scrutiny of the data it’s required to provide to federal regulators. Meanwhile, Waymo has published several studies in peer-reviewed journals. Recently, the nonprofit Insurance Institute for Highway Safety examined Waymo’s first 50 million miles of fully autonomous driving across multiple cities and concluded that its crash rates were significantly lower than those of human drivers. The Cybercab launch comes at an odd moment for Tesla. Whereas other vehicle launches have excited Tesla’s many fans with their cutting-edge technology, the Cybercab remains a bit of a curiosity. It’s the lightest, most efficient electric vehicle Tesla has ever produced. But it’s unclear whether the technology powering it is adequate for commercial operations. Still, it’s more like the Tesla Semi than the Model Y or Cybertruck, insofar as it seems destined for commercial service and not personal ownership — despite Musk’s claims that you will eventually be able to buy one. The Cybercab’s lack of traditional controls means it will be hamstrung by federal safety rules that require things like pedals and side mirrors before they can be sold to the public. That said, if Tesla were to receive an exemption from federal regulators, allowing the company to produce and sell thousands of Cybercabs, that calculus could change. Amazon’s Zoox recently received permission to begin charging for rides in its purpose-built robotaxi. Whether Tesla is also seeking a similar exemption is unknown. What is known is that Tesla is going to roll out the Cybercab later this month, as if it’s really ready for primetime. But lingering safety questions, as well as the limited nature of Tesla’s Robotaxi service, suggests the Cybercab may still have a long road ahead of it.

articles.title: This tiny, magnetic e-reader could stop you from doomscrolling
articles.summary: The Xteink X3 is a delightfully tiny, MagSafe-compatible e-ink reader that attaches to the back of your phone like a Pop Socket.
articles.body:
It was love at first sight. It felt like scouring the mall, dipping in and out of sprawling department stores in search of a specific, elusive item, only to finally find what you’re looking for. Only, I didn’t even know I was searching for something like the Xteink X3 , because I never dared dream of something so delightful: a tiny, MagSafe-compatible e-ink reader that could attach to my iPhone like a Pop Socket.

This was it. My life would change forever. I would get my hands on the Xteink X3, and I would stop doomscrolling forever. I would read more books than ever before… which is saying something, since — brag — I read at least 50 books a year. But — not a brag — I probably spend even more time on social media than I do reading. I know that I feel generally less anxious when I limit my social media time, but alas, the siren song of TikTok beckons me. What if instead of opening social media, I could just flip my phone over and read on a tiny, Kindle-like e-ink screen? Could this $80 gadget fix me?

Since we first published this review in May, Xteink released the X4 Pro, which adds a touchscreen and a front light. Find out what I thought of it here . It’s $99 from Xteink’s website , while the older model is now discounted to $69 at Amazon .

I’ve tried reading books (… or downloads from AO3 ) on my phone, immersing myself in a fictional world, rather than posts from the president in which he threatens to obliterate an entire country . But something about looking at my phone, where I’m constantly tempted to open Instagram to see whatever Reel someone sent me, doesn’t quite soothe me the way that a book or an e-ink device like a Kindle does.

I was so excited for my X3 to arrive that I constantly refreshed the tracking link until finally, it was delivered. Even though I had meticulously compared the dimensions of the X3 to my iPhone 16, or my Pop Socket wallet, I still worried it might not fit — the previous model, the Xteink X4 (basically the same device but a little bigger) only fit on larger phones like the iPhone Pro Max line. But sure enough, the X3 magnetically attached to the back of my phone like it was custom-made to fit.

My X3 came in the mail about two hours before I had to leave to go to a Phillies game, so I rushed to load books onto it, because I thought it would be really funny to take photos in which I read “The Power Broker” in a crowded baseball stadium. Behold, my handiwork:

For the first several days that I had the X3, I carried it with me on the back of my phone. This made me a bit nervous, though, since I’m used to having a Pop Socket wallet, which means I’ve gotten in the habit of leaving home without my actual wallet. But I found that I used the X3 just as much when I carried it in my purse or pocket, rather than attaching it to my phone. I’m still not sure if I’ll keep this setup, or if I’ll start actually using a real wallet so that I can attach the e-reader, but for now, that’s what has felt most natural. Plus, my X3 shipped with a very compact, cute, magnetic case, which perfectly protects the device and its screen and makes it a little easier to hold. At just $9 for the case, I’d recommend getting one. The case can also magnetize to your phone, though it feels a bit less secure than attaching your X3 alone.

Over my two weeks of testing, I did find that the X3 helped me read more. If you’re in line at a coffee shop, or waiting for the bus, you can just pull out the e-reader instead of opening Instagram. I didn’t find the small screen difficult to read on, either. But just buying the device won’t change your habits — you have to remember that you have a 3.7-inch screen in your pocket that can fit hundreds of books.

The Xteink X3 is pretty close to being the device of my dreams, but it’s not quite there yet. The firmware that the device comes with is pretty clunky — not unusable, but not exactly intuitive. I expected this, since the Xteink Reddit community was buzzing about CrossPoint , a community-made, free, open source firmware. The process of downloading CrossPoint was a bit intimidating as someone who writes words, rather than code — but with the instructions on CrossPoint’s website (and a few videos), it was easy enough. I encountered some difficulties at first, but then I realized it was because I was trying to download the X4 firmware onto my X3, so… my bad. You probably won’t even need the YouTube videos!

When you start loading books and open source firmware onto your X3, you’ll notice another divisive aspect of the device: It doesn’t have a USB-C port, unlike the X4. Instead, it uses a magnetic charger. Yes, it’s annoying to have yet another charging cable specifically for this one device, but I don’t care that much. After two weeks of consistent use, my X3 has dropped from a 100% charge to a 96% charge, so I can’t imagine I’ll be using that magnetic charger too often. You don’t even need the cord to add new books to your e-reader — you can transfer files over Wi-Fi from your phone or computer (I wouldn’t call the process user-friendly, but I was able to figure it out without Googling anything).

Speaking of loading books, that’s another drawback. The majority of what I read on my Kindle comes from Libby, which is my favorite app (#notsponsored). The Libby app allows you to easily borrow e-books or audiobooks from your library and send them to your Kindle. But you can’t get those e-books (legally) onto an Xteink e-reader, since libraries use protected versions of .epub files that deter users from copying them (you also can’t read books you buy from Amazon’s e-book store on non-Amazon devices, because capitalism). This lack of compatibility is a drawback, but it also makes the device feel unique — it’s a “dumb” device that has no apps and no touch screen, which feels startlingly refreshing in an era of AI-enabled refrigerators.

It’s not hard to find interesting .epub files to load onto the X3, even if you can’t access your Kindle library or Libby. A lot of great books are in the public domain, which means that they’re no longer subject to copyright and can be downloaded for free (I’ve weirdly never read “Pride and Prejudice,” so the time is now). A few months ago, I bought the entire .epub catalogs of sci-fi writers Charlie Jane Anders and Annalee Newitz as part of a charity fundraiser, which should keep me busy for quite a bit. If you wanted to, you could even turn online articles or blogs into .epubs using a free program like Calibre .

So, did the Xteink X3 fix me? Am I now a newly reformed woman who has a healthy relationship with social media and has read a bunch of classic novels that I never read as an English major, since I mostly took classes with ridiculous titles like “Aestheticus Extremus: The Politics of Precarious Invention in North American Poetry and Poetics”? It’s not that simple. But if you meet the X3 halfway and make a concerted effort to use it, then maybe you’ll spare yourself from a bit more brain rot.

articles.title: Let’s take a look at the retro tech making a comeback | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Boom boxes, instant cameras, and even landlines are making a comeback. Here are the coolest retro-inspired devices available.
articles.body:
From blasting music on a boom box to watching a photo develop in your hands, many people are rediscovering the imperfect charm of older gadgets that smartphones and laptops just can’t replicate.

Tech companies are leaning all the way in, blending nostalgic design with modern functionality. Here are some of the coolest retro-inspired devices out there right now.

In a world full of endless notifications, tabs, doomscrolling, and other distractions, smart typewriters are carving out a niche for a more focused writing experience. These devices strip things back to the essentials: just you, a keyboard, and your words.

Freewrite ( $699 ): Freewrite features a design inspired by classic typewriters, providing a minimalist writing experience. It includes a small screen and satisfying keys to press. However, if you need to make edits, your drafts are synced to the cloud and can be exported to any software.

Pomera ($549): A more modern take than Freewrite’s device, Pomera looks like a compact laptop and includes helpful tools like spell check, document management, and word counts. With multiple transfer options and up to 20 hours of battery life, it balances simplicity with functionality.

Boom boxes, cassette tapes, and record players

The boom box is re-emerging as both a design statement and a functional audio device. Today’s versions pair chunky buttons, cassette decks, and oversized speakers with modern upgrades like Bluetooth and rechargeable batteries. Cassette players, meanwhile, are also reappearing with enhancements, and record players continue to be popular as well.

We Are Rewind ($525): A modern reimagining of the classic boom box, the GB-001 has everything you desire in a boom box, but better. It keeps all the essential features, such as woofers, tweeters, a cassette player, and recorder, while adding Bluetooth and a rechargeable battery. With speakers delivering 104 W of power, it’s built for both nostalgia and high-quality sound.

Bumpboxx : Now live on Kickstarter, the new BB-777 is a portable boom box that has a bold ’80s aesthetic while packing in a wide range of features. It includes a powerful three-way speaker system, dual cassette decks with recording and high-speed dubbing, a built-in CD player, USB recording, and more. It also supports multiband radio, including AM and FM.

Retrospekt ($99): A minimalist take on the classic Walkman-style player, this portable cassette device features all the essentials: play, rewind, fast-forward, and record. It supports both battery power and USB-C, making it a simple but modern throwback.

Kickback World ($500): This DEKO record player started shipping in January 2025 and has become popular not just for being a step up from traditional players, but also for aesthetic appeal with its orange acrylic, “Swedish modernism” design compared to the traditional, suitcase-style record players we normally see.

There’s something uniquely satisfying about holding a physical photo seconds after taking it. That sense of excitement and anticipation, combined with the imperfect beauty of film, makes each shot feel more meaningful than a quick snap on your iPhone.

Polaroid ($249) : Polaroid has never stopped being popular, but it’s always innovating. Most recently, the Polaroid Flip launched last year, a retro-looking instant camera with modern features like autofocus and app connectivity for remote control.

Fujifilm ($225) : If you want a hybrid camera that lets you shoot digitally and print photos, then there’s the Fujifilm Instax Mini Evo . It offers the best of both worlds: instant film with the flexibility of digital storage and sharing. In recent years, the device received an upgrade with USB-C. In January, Fujifilm launched a new variant, the Instax Mini Evo Cinema ($412) , a three-in-one hybrid camera that can even print images from your smartphone.

Kodak ($30) : You also can’t go wrong with a classic single-use, disposable camera. It’s simple, reliable, and still delivers quality photos without needing any photography skills. Last year, Kodak released a miniature keychain digital camera, the “Charmera.” A twist on its signature “Fling” camera, this tiny device can save and transfer photos and videos using a USB-C cable.

Landline phones are making a quiet comeback, especially among people seeking a break from screen-heavy communication. They’re also gaining popularity as aesthetic objects, often used as statement pieces in home décor.

Tin Can ($100): Remember the days when you would rush home after school to use the landline and chat with your friends for hours? That’s the inspiration behind Tin Can. Designed for kids, it resembles a landline phone but doesn’t require a phone jack, just Wi-Fi. Only approved people can call, and parents can easily manage contacts through a companion app. You can preorder now. There’s a free plan to call other Tin Can users and a $9.99/month plan for calling all approved contacts.

Clicks ($499): Announced at CES 2026 , hardware company Clicks Technology debuted its smartphone that looks a lot like a BlackBerry, which dominated the phone market back in the 2000s and has seen a revival among Gen Z. While Clicks’ phone has access to text messaging and productivity apps like Gmail and Slack, it doesn’t provide access to mobile games and social media, making it an enticing alternative for people looking to go back to the good old days.
